# Pulse — agent operating guide

## Inventory vocabulary primer

## Estate config at a glance

Pulse is driven by one declarative estate-config YAML that you edit. It targets schema major v1. You never touch a host to change monitoring — you edit this file and re-render (see the invariants guide). The reference estate under `examples/reference/estate/estate.yaml` is the worked example this pack teaches from.

## Top-level sections

The estate-config declares these top-level sections (schema order):
- `estate`: Estate-wide identity and defaults — the fleet name plus fallbacks other sections inherit.
- `hosts`: The machines under management, each tagged with a collection_class that fixes how Pulse reaches and probes it.
- `services`: The workloads to watch on those hosts — what 'healthy' means and which probes prove it.
- `channels`: Where alerts are delivered (chat, email, webhook), referenced by name from routing.
- `routing_overrides`: Per-target exceptions to default severity routing — send a given entity's alerts to a specific channel.
- `suppressions`: Deliberate, rationale-bearing silences — an entity is intentionally unmonitored for a stated reason.

## Host collection classes

Every host declares exactly one collection class, which fixes how Pulse collects from it:
- `excluded`
- `hypervisor-api`
- `managed-linux`
- `nas-api`
- `probe-only`

Pick the class that matches how the host exposes itself (a Linux exporter, a hypervisor/NAS API, a black-box probe, or an explicit exclusion).

## Deep-health & backup-freshness

A service may declare a `deep_health` probe (endpoint + response_mapping + alert_expression) or a `backup_freshness` spec (signal + threshold). In the reference estate the `portal-web` service attaches a `deep_health` probe and `nas-backups` attaches a `backup_freshness` spec — copy those shapes:

```yaml
services:
  - name: portal-web
    host: harbor-web-01
    kind: http
    deep_health:
      endpoint: https://portal.aurora.example/api/health
      alert_expression: pulse_deep_health_status == 0
      credential: ${WEB_HEALTH_TOKEN}   # env reference, never a literal
```

## Command signals (host-computed backup freshness)

A `backup_freshness` spec with a `threshold` alone is a declaration-only alert threshold — it delivers no live series. Add a **`command`** and Pulse delivers it through the command-exporter: the renderer synthesizes a `scalar` command-signal on the service's host emitting `pulse_backup_freshness_age_seconds{service}` (the value) and `pulse_backup_freshness_up{service}` (`1` ok / `0` blind — missing data is never a healthy backup). The command must be read-only argv (run verbatim, no shell) that prints the age of the newest backup artifact, in **seconds**, to stdout. The service must resolve to a `managed-linux` host — that is the only class that runs the command-exporter bundle; a `command` on any other class is a validation error.

```yaml
services:
  - name: nas-backups
    host: backup-orchestrator-01          # must be a managed-linux host
    kind: backup
    backup_freshness:
      signal: pulse_backup_freshness_age_seconds
      threshold: "24h"
      command: ["/opt/pulse/backup-age", "/mnt/backups"]  # prints newest-backup AGE in seconds
      interval: "15m"                     # optional; default 15m
```

## Channels, routing & suppressions

Channels carry a credential reference and define where alerts go. Each channel has a `kind` (`chat`, `email`, `push`, `telegram`, or `webhook`). A `telegram` channel adds one required non-secret knob — `options.chat_id` (an int64 chat id or `@name`) — alongside its credential; the renderer emits it to an Alertmanager `telegram_configs` receiver with the credential as `bot_token` and `chat_id` carried verbatim from `options`. `routing_overrides` map a severity to specific channels. A `suppressions` entry silences a target, but every suppression requires an explicit `rationale` — silence is never anonymous (see the invariants guide).

```yaml
channels:
  - name: ops-telegram
    kind: telegram
    credential: ${TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}   # bot token — a reference, never a literal
    options:
      chat_id: "-1001234567890"        # required for telegram; non-secret
```

## Layers: generated base + hand-authored overlay

A source file may carry an optional top-level `layer:` so a machine-generated skeleton and hand-authored monitoring policy live side by side in the same estate directory. `layer: base` is the regenerable, deterministic skeleton (intrinsic facts a generator knows — hosts, addresses); `layer: overlay` is the human-owned refinement. The loader deep-merges them by identity (same host/service/channel `name`, or the `estate` block) with the **overlay winning** every conflict — except a conflicting array (e.g. `exporter_ports`), where the overlay array replaces the base array whole. `layer:` is opt-in: a repo with no markers behaves exactly as before (every source implicitly `base`, a duplicate identity still a hard error). Commit the base, the overlay, and the rendered tree together, and gate with `pulse render --check` (exit 0 = the committed tree still equals a fresh render).

```yaml
# estate/00-skeleton.base.yaml — machine-generated, regenerable
layer: base
hosts:
  - name: app-01
    collection_class: managed-linux
    exporter_ports: [9100]
---
# estate/10-monitoring.overlay.yaml — you own this by hand
layer: overlay
hosts:
  - name: app-01              # same identity → deep-merged onto the base host
    cadvisor: true            # overlay scalar wins
    exporter_ports: [9100, 9256]   # overlay array REPLACES the base array whole
```

## Secret grammar

Credentials are ALWAYS a reference — `${ENV_VAR}` or `op://vault/item/field` — never an inline secret literal. If you ever see a raw token or password in a file, stop and flag it to the operator.


## Operate loop

## The operate loop

You operate Pulse by editing the estate-config and running the CLI verbs in order. The loop is:

1. `pulse init`  →  2. `pulse render`  →  3. `pulse validate`  →  4. `pulse coverage`

Start with `init` once (scaffolds this pack), then cycle author → `validate` → `render` → `coverage` on every change.

## Verbs

- `pulse init` — Scaffold a Pulse repo (config + estate + guidance pack), create-only.
- `pulse render` — Materialize the estate into the committed rendered/ tree.
- `pulse validate` — Load + validate the estate against the inventory schema.
- `pulse coverage` — Report covered / gaps / suppressed entities for the estate.

## Exit codes

Every verb follows the 0/1/2 contract: 0 clean, 1 a finding/gap/drift you must act on, 2 a fault (bad input or internal error). Per verb:

### `pulse init`
- exit 0: scaffold written (or idempotent under --force)
- exit 1: an existing target would be clobbered without --force (wouldClobber)
- exit 2: a path escapes repo root / a raw fs fault

### `pulse render`
- exit 0: render clean (write mode, or --check with no drift)
- exit 1: --check with drift
- exit 2: a thrown tool fault

### `pulse validate`
- exit 0: validate clean
- exit 1: a seeded error finding (or a warning under --strict)
- exit 2: a thrown tool fault

### `pulse coverage`
- exit 0: no gaps
- exit 1: one or more declared-but-unmonitored gaps
- exit 2: a thrown tool fault

## Reading --json

Add `--json` to any verb for a machine `PulseEnvelope<D>` with top-level fields: `ok`, `exitCode`, `command`, `findings`, `data`, `meta`. Key off `exitCode` and, per verb, the `data` field names:
- `init`: `created`, `skipped`, `wouldClobber`
- `render`: `outputRoot`, `filesWritten`, `mode`, `drift`
- `validate`: (no data payload)
- `coverage`: `covered`, `gaps`, `suppressed`

## Worked run

The estate dir is cwd-relative (there is no flag to override it), so `cd` into the estate first:

```bash
cd examples/reference
pulse validate --json    # exit 0 clean; 1 on a finding; 2 on a fault
pulse render
pulse coverage --json    # exit 1 if a declared target is unmonitored
```


## Invariants & guardrails

## The three invariants

These hold on every task, without exception:

1. **Render ≠ deploy.** Nothing you run in this repo touches a host.
2. **Secret references, never literals.** Credentials are `${ENV}` / `op://` refs only.
3. **Silence requires a rationale.** No target is excluded or suppressed without one.

## Render ≠ deploy

`pulse render`, `pulse validate`, and `pulse coverage` never touch a host — they only read and write files in this repo. Any change to a host (installing an agent, wiring alert channels, enrolling backups) happens ONLY in a supervised runbook session. You propose the estate-config edit; a human runs the matching runbook (see the operator tooling index).

## Secret references, never literals

Every credential in the estate-config is a **reference**, resolved at deploy time. Never paste a raw token, password, or key into any file:

```yaml
credential: ${WEB_HEALTH_TOKEN}          # environment reference
credential: op://infra/nas/token         # 1Password reference
```

## Silence requires a rationale

A host or target is only excluded (collection class `excluded`) or suppressed with an explicit `rationale` field in the estate-config. Silent suppression is forbidden — if you drop a target from monitoring, the config must say why, so a reviewer can see the intent.

## If in doubt

When a task would require touching a host, deleting a file, or inlining a secret, stop and escalate to the human operator rather than take a destructive or host-touching action. Proposing the estate edit is always safe; applying it to a host is not yours to do.

## Skills & subagents

This pack scaffolds these operator tools. Reach for them in-repo (they never touch a host):

| Tool | Kind | Reach for it when… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `estate-authoring` | skill | You need to add a host, service, or deep-health probe to the estate-config. |
| `render-validate-coverage` | skill | You need to run a verb and act on its exit code / `--json`. |
| `coverage-interpretation` | skill | You have a coverage gap to explain and close inline. |
| `alert-triage` | subagent | A firing alert needs classifying by severity and routing. |
| `coverage-interpreter` | subagent | You want to hand off a full `coverage --json` payload for per-gap analysis. |

## Runbooks (host-write sessions)

Host writes — installing agents, wiring channels, enrolling backups — happen ONLY in a supervised runbook session under `docs/runbooks/`. You propose the estate edit; a human runs the runbook. The runbooks:

| Runbook | File | Reach for it when… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bootstrap | `bootstrap.md` | Standing up a fresh Pulse engine on a host. |
| Agent install | `agent-install.md` | Enrolling the host-agent bundle on a monitored host. |
| Rollout session | `rollout-session.md` | The supervised session wiring alert channels + deadman. |
| Backup enrollment | `backup-enrollment.md` | Declaring backup freshness and wiring its rules. |
| Retirement checklist | `retirement-checklist.md` | Cutting a host/system over off the incumbent monitor. |

## Decision guide

- Editing the estate-config → the `estate-authoring` skill.
- A `validate` / `render` / `coverage` question → the `render-validate-coverage` skill.
- A coverage gap to explain → the `coverage-interpretation` skill (or hand the whole `coverage --json` payload to the `coverage-interpreter` subagent).
- A firing alert → the `alert-triage` subagent.
- Touching a host → the matching runbook above, supervised by a human. Never do it from the repo yourself.
